texts: The Millau Viaduct in Aveyron, southern France - Eve Livesey/Moment Unreleased RF
China is in the process of building the world’s largest dam (the

) – a mammoth undertaking that is, perhaps unsurprisingly, causing much controversy amid its neighbours. Then again, vast engineering projects are often problematic (just look at the Itaipu Dam in Brazil). But they are also inspiring, huge, overwhelming spectacles which bear witness to what science and technology (and a lot of concrete) can achieve on a grand scale.
and tunnels that cross Sydney’s harbour, the Oresund Crossing between Sweden and Denmark, or futuristic highways such as

or Germany’s autobahn, these behemoths of human endeavour thrill us. We flock to them on our travels, craving the sense of being simultaneously dwarfed and awed by what could readily be described as the world’s greatest man-made wonders.
Here is our choice of the 10 most magnificent major engineering marvels around the world.
The Panama Canal has a gruelling but impressive construction history - Danny Lehman/Stone RF

feels genuinely exotic. You’re aware of the failed attempts to build this true marvel, the devastating impact that tropical diseases had on the builders, and the sheer scope of the project to blast mountains and link lakes. Admire the massive canal from the Radisson Panama Canal, a Ballardian scene with a deserted swimming pool and eerie colonial reminders – like old drive-thrus – of when the US ran the Panama Canal Zone and marshalled the little trains that yank the giant ships along the water. Weird and wonderful.
from London Heathrow to Panama City via Houston.
A British and French worker meeting during the breakthrough of the Channel Tunnel in 1990, 40m below the seabed - API/Getty Images

(cordial agreement) concrete by linking France to Britain had been a dream for a century. It finally came true when the Channel Tunnel opened in 1994, transforming the way we travel with Eurostar and Le Shuttle services. During construction there was a visitor centre at Cheriton, but today the perfect place to appreciate those

This slice of new land beneath Kent’s white cliffs was created from the spoil of the Nineties tunnel diggers. It’s perfect for picnics and birdwatching – and near the terminal outside Folkestone if you want to break your journey to the Dordogne for a few hours. Folkestone has plenty of new restaurants for lunch, including
, as well as hip, renovated pubs such as
from London St Pancras to Folkestone.
The Akashi-Kaikyo Bridge successfully withstood a powerful earthquake in 1995, while it was still under construction - Sean Pavone/iStockphoto

Japan’s ambition to connect its main archipelago was a bold and brazen one that involved tunnels and bridges spanning impossibly deep channels and complex topography. Oh, and did we mention the earthquakes? This resilient nation really popped the champagne corks when the Akashi-Kaikyo Bridge was opened in 1998, spanning the strait between Honshu and Awaji Island, and linking Shikoku with Kobe and the rest of Metropolitan Japan. A decade in the making,
it is worth seeing this bridge
on a day out from Kobe – if only to say you’ve witnessed one of the world’s longest spans.
from London Heathrow to Kobe via Taipei.
The Millau Viaduct crosses the river Tarn - Michael Reinhard

At one stage the world’s tallest bridge, it’s the incredible height of the Millau Viaduct that gets you. There are observation areas where you can park to see the top of the viaduct, which often pokes up above the clouds and mist. It can get very windy up here because of the eccentric micro-climate of the gorge.

Walk down into that valley if you really want to feel awe, and see where the concrete legs of the motorway bridge slam into the Occitanian soil and cross the river Tarn. Norman Foster was responsible for the elegant design (along with French engineer Michel Virlogeux), and the viaduct opened in 2004 as part of the A75 Autoroute.
Break the drive from Britain with a night at
from London Gatwick or Manchester to Montpellier.
Beijing – Shanghai High Speed Railway, China
The high-speed rail line between Shanghai and Beijing was the longest of its kind when it was unveiled in 2011 - Peng Wang/iStockphoto
Shanghai is full of impressive modern engineering, including one of the world’s handful of
which glide from Pudong airport to the city in minutes, powered by magnets. Another notable Chinese transport achievement is the high-speed rail line which runs from Shanghai up to Beijing.

At more than 800 miles, it was the longest high-speed rail line built in one go when it opened in 2011 – taking just three years to construct. Anyone associated with HS2 please look away now. Enjoying the line and its deft ability to traverse the Yangtze Delta is easy – just buy a ticket on your phone and choose how flash you would like your class of seat (and service) to be for the four-hour journey.
, just outside central Shanghai, has doubles from £79.

The art deco Hoover Dam makes it a worthwhile visit from Las Vegas - Alina Rudya/Bell Collective

in China may currently be the world’s biggest – and unquestionably awe-inspiring – but the art deco swagger of the Hoover Dam is hard to beat. The Dam and Lake Mead behind it allowed southern California and Las Vegas to grow into the behemoths they are today, and provided work during the Great Depression. The dam is a real work of art as well as being an engineering marvel. It’s a simple
, and a new bypass bridge means you can easily park up and walk to a viewing spot for great photos. If you want to get closer to the action, there is a visitors’ centre and tours.
in Las Vegas has doubles from £228.
from London Heathrow to Las Vegas.
German autobahns are a thrill to drive on, with landmarks like the Frankfurter Kreuz showcasing the scale of the network - Joerg Hackemann / Alamy Stock Photo

Germany is chock full of engineering marvels, such as the Kiel Canal and the Wuppertal Schweberbahn. But pelting along the autobahn remains the stuff of dreams for many drivers, and with the centenary of its inception in Frankfurt taking place this year, there’s never been a more fitting time to do it. The Frankfurter Kreuz is an impressive intersection that ranks among Europe’s busiest and oldest, while in Berlin, the A115 through Grunewald, comprises the former AVUS race track. Without (many) speed limits or any tolls, driving these innovative roads is a great deal more fun than their ruinously pricey Spanish or French counterparts.
from London Luton to Dortmund and rent a car.
Lisbon’s spectacular Aguas Livres Aqueduct is on UNESCO’s Tentative List for World Heritage status - iStockphoto

Where would we be without water? Especially in hot, dry cities like Lisbon. This incredible piece of engineering – currently on UNESCO’s Tentative List for World Heritage status – solved that very problem by bringing fresh water from the mountains around Lisbon down into the city for residents to drink.

Dating back to the 1700s, this beautiful structure is still standing and you can even walk over some parts of it, marvelling at how it crosses the Alcantara valley at up to 213 feet in height. The aqueduct ends at the spooky-but-spellbinding Mother of Water Reservoir (Mãe d’Água das Amoreiras) in the Amoreiras neighbourhood. Go in and imagine how it’s transformed for special events, like when they project art on the walls. The V rooftop bar at nearby Vintage is perfect for a drink after your walk.
to Lisbon from London Heathrow, Gatwick and Manchester.
Port Vell in Barcelona is an excellent example of successful urban planning and waterfront integration - Scott E Barbour

Barcelona’s waterfront is just a series of engineering marvels hiding in plain sight. The beaches we all love were created by importing truckloads of sand and building huge breakwaters to keep it all there. The recently rebuilt Port Olímpic was dug out and opened just before the 1992 Olympic Games and crowned with the swish
rising above it, where you can head for a fancy vermouth cocktail.

The B10 Ronda Litoral Ring Road was built to link venues during the Games, but most of it is cleverly sunk in a tunnel with playgrounds and parks above, so it doesn’t cut off the routes to the sea. The Parc Fòrum, meanwhile, was built for a 2004 cultural exhibition, a sprawling concrete site which makes an ideal site for the
Festival every spring. Primavera’s after-parties happen by the pool at the
’s new flight from London Luton to Barcelona.
Dramatic dams, ditches and dykes, The Netherlands
The Afsluitdijk creates a massive freshwater reservoir, vital for drinking water and farming irrigation - GM/iStockphoto

The Dutch were so good at dykes that the British invited them over to drain the Fens. Their knowledge of fighting the sea and reclaiming land is a real sight to behold. The Delta Works are worth exploring – huge dams and sluices you can cycle along (watch out for the wind) in the south of the country, protecting against storms and floods.

The Afsluitdijk in the north, meanwhile, is truly mind-bending – at more than 20 miles long, you can’t see the end of this massive pile of earth which turned the sea into a freshwater lake, the IJmeer, when it was dammed. It all allowed massive amounts of “polder” – new land reclaimed from water – to be created, and transformed the country.
from London to Amsterdam. Book local trains around the Netherlands to explore the dams with

texts: Japan’s Himeji Castle is said to resemble a bird in flight - Alamy
Which of the world’s man-made creations merit jet fumes, bumpy roads and holidaying hordes to ogle and touch? My list is below. Yours may differ, but I would proffer two ideas.

Firstly, there is wisdom in crowds. Clichés are clichés for a reason. If everyone says it is wondrous and beautiful, statistically, you will probably agree. What humans find moving and marvellous is remarkably predictable. Don’t fear mass appeal.

Secondly, if in doubt go sacred. Many of the world’s most transporting buildings are religious, self-consciously juxtaposing great scale with coherent detail and ornament to evoke the eternal. Buildings that successfully dignify the human condition move us in ways that buildings that honestly express their construction never can.
Great Pyramid of Giza, Egypt, c.2560 BC
The Great Pyramid of Giza is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World - Anadolu via Getty Images/Murat Gok

The photos cannot do it. You know them too well. You have to visit to be awestruck by the sheer scale of the thing. Herodotus related that 100,000 labourers took 20 years to pull and pile the stone, for him a textbook example of cruel non-Greek ways. Standing minuscule beside the oldest and only surviving of the Seven Wonders of the World, you can understand.
Inside Rome’s magnificent Pantheon - iStockphoto/Vladislav Zolotov
There is nowhere greater to stand than directly under the oculus at the centre of

peerless Pantheon. The dome is the largest unreinforced concrete dome that has or will ever be created. It is a mingled miracle of heavenly symbolism and earthly engineering. Coffers, hidden internal chambers and porous pumice stone lighten the central load where the dome is most vulnerable to collapse.

The best way to preserve a building is to sanctify and use it, not pickle it in unchanging “heritage”. The Pantheon survives because the former temple became a church in AD 609 and has been continually repaired ever since. Astonishingly, the original bronze Roman doors still serve. Outside, immense granite Egyptian columns stand sentry, seemingly for eternity.
Hagia Sophia is a monument of Byzantine architecture and art - skaman306/Teerayut Chaisarn
No building stands as firmly at the crossroads of history, geography, religion and civilisation as Hagia Sophia. The Byzantine Empire’s former

, site of a church for over a millennium, yanked violently into a new life as the Ottomans’ great mosque after the 1453 sack of Constantinople, a museum for 85 years after the secularising Kemal Atatürk, the Hagia Sophia has been redesignated as a mosque since 2020. Like the nearby Bosphorus, history eddies past.

I will never forget entering for the first time: the huge and spreading pendentive dome (the world’s first at this scale), the sudden dark after the sunshine outside, receding as my eyes adjusted and the golden mosaics, colours, basket capitals, saints and angels emerged from the stygian gloom.
Ely Cathedral’s Octagon Tower - Alamy/Martin Bache

Rising above the frigid East Anglian fens, Ely’s greatest glory grew from catastrophe. In 1322 its Norman crossing tower collapsed. It was replaced with an oak octagon, lead-covered from above, luminous from below, which is unparalleled in any church in any nation. Unusually we know the names of the architect and carpenter who conceived and shaped this miracle: Alan of Walsingham and William Hurley.
Piazza San Marco, Venice, 11th to 16th centuries
Piazza San Marco is the historic heart of Venice - Moment RF
Not St Mark’s sinuous Basilica, nor the
, heavy with Republican power, not the towering Campanile, nor the delicate Logetta, not the elaborate Clocktower, nor the Piazzetta with its heart-stopping lagoon views, not Sansovino’s proud Zecca
nor the enveloping Ala Napoleonica which finalises the enclosure, but all of it, every brick and stone and column of it, make Piazza San Marco, the world’s greatest town square.

It defies words. It defines urban beauty. Even Napoleon, no romantic, who gaily murdered the Venetian Republic, was moved to wonder by the place. Its buildings drip with riches. My favourite is the porphyry statue of the four tetrarchs. You can sit beside and touch their toes.
Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world - Moment RF/Tumjang

No single edifice challenged European assumptions of their own cultural superiority as effortlessly as this 12th-century, initially Hindu, now Buddhist, temple city (the name’s meaning) emerging from the Cambodian forests.

Imagine the stupefaction of an early 16th-century Portuguese visitor: “It is not possible to describe it with a pen... it is like no other building in the world.” A Victorian added: “It is grander than anything left to us by Greece or Rome.” Angkor Wat is the world’s largest religious complex and, uniquely in this list, features on its nation’s flag.
Sainte-Chapelle’s ceilings feature deep blue ribbed arches decorated with golden stars - RooM RF/RilindH
former royal chapel, commissioned by Louis IX to rhyme with royal chapels in Venice, Aachen and Constantinople.

Emerging via a tight spiral staircase from the ill-lit lower chapel into Sainte Chapelle is a passage from night to day, from earth to heaven, from sin to salvation. Polychromatic light scatters through the vast rayonnant windows with their web of bar-tracery. The bright blue ceiling twinkles with a thousand painted stars. Don’t forget to breathe.
Revolutionary thugs vandalised the chapel in the 18th century, but fortunately 19th-century French Gothicists, including a young Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, restored it with love and colour.
Clermont-Ferrand Cathedral is built entirely in black Volvic lava stone - benkrut

Most Gothic cathedrals climb into the clouds with pinnacles of pale stone. Clermont does it in black. Begun in 1248, Notre-Dame-de-l’Assomption is built from the dark volcanic lava of nearby Volvic, its twin spires rising over an equally volcanic landscape.
The second surprise is inside. Against almost black piers, medieval stained glass ignites in reds, blues, greens and golds: colours made brighter by the surrounding darkness.
Brunelleschi’s Dome is an iconic Renaissance structure - Suttipong Sutiratanachai
It does not matter whether buildings are too big. It matters if they are too ugly. Florence Cathedral took 140 years to build. You can see why. It dominates the still physically
leering over its medieval streets or suddenly blocking the vista as you turn a corner. Nobody minds. The delicate marble panels in alternating white, green or pink are too beautiful for complaint.
Above it all rises Brunelleschi’s Dome, reaching for the heavens and announcing that mankind had achieved again the lost knowledge of the ancients.
Beijing’s Forbidden City is an imperial palace complex of the Ming and Qing dynasties - Moment RF/Jackyenjoyphotography
Strictly, this is not one building but 980, with 8,886 rooms.

Forbidden City is a labyrinth within a city within a city: a vast, symmetrical sequence of courts, gates and halls laid out along an imperial axis, the scale reducing as you progress from the expansive to the intimate.

Its other genius is colour. Vermilion walls and columns, the colour of fire, blaze beneath yellow-glazed roofs, the emperor’s colour, while blue, green and gold crowd the painted brackets beneath. Built for the Ming emperors, this is hierarchy, procession and etiquette frozen into bricks and tiles.
Chateau de Chenonceau, Loire Valley, mid 16th century
Chateau de Chenonceau was built on the foundations of an old watermill - Alamy/JHVEPhoto
The Chateau de Chambord is bigger and more illustrious, but no French chateau catches the breath as effortlessly as Chenonceau.

A rich cream cake of flamboyant Gothic forms and Renaissance classical solecisms, Chenonceau is not just a building but a bridge over the river Cher, whose rippling and reflecting waters double the number of oriel and oeil-de-boeuf windows visible from the riverbanks. It is ludicrously romantic.

The chateau, an escape route between Nazi-occupied and Vichy France in war, was unkindly treated by the 20th century. Flooded and bombed, it is now miraculously renatured, a renaissance chateau in date and deed.
Himeji Castle surrounded by cherry blossom - Alamy/Jui-Chi Chan
Military buildings should not look so good. Himeji is a great white apparition of layered roofs and plastered walls, earning its nickname White Heron Castle.

Beauty conceals purpose. Gates, narrow passages and bewildering turns were designed to confuse attackers as they climbed towards the keep. Yet the whole defensive machine seems almost weightless, like a bird about to take flight.
The Taj Mahal was made a Unesco World Heritage Site in 1983 - adamkaz
Description seems superfluous so iconic is the world’s greatest witness to love, Shah Jahan’s tomb for his late wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
Everyone recognises this marble marvel with its sinuous central dome and its four surrounding smaller domes or

. But the genius of the thing is in the detail from up close not just the form from afar. Inlays, tessellations, interlocking patterns, plant motifs, four-pointed stars and elaborate lattice windows abound. They are somehow both overwhelming and restrained. First visiting as a cynical 19-year-old, I was dumbstruck.
Castle Howard appeared as Evelyn Waugh’s Brideshead on screen - CAG Photography Ltd/Charlotte Graham

No building could be less typical of the dour Yorkshire temperament than the 3rd Earl of Carlisle’s flamboyant, almost megalomaniac, palace. Sir John Vanbrugh and Nicholas Hawksmoor’s first collaboration and masterpiece is too princely to be convincingly English.

as Evelyn Waugh’s tragic Brideshead, in the 1981 TV series. Devastated by fire in 1940, had the modern National Trust owned it, it would have been left a ruin. Instead, it is slowly being rediscovered.
Neuschwanstein is the world’s tallest castle - Alamy /Alpineguide

is the Platonic idea of a romantic castle. Straddling two steep cliffs in the Alpine foothills, the world’s tallest castle is crammed, inside and out, with turrets, pinnacles, lancets, gables and sculptures. It is all a gleeful fake, a medieval castle built in the 19th-century age of iron with borrowed money by Ludwig II, one of the last Bavarian kings.
La Sagrada Família, Gaudí‘s magnum opus - Sylvain Sonnet
Begun in 1882 as a conventional Gothic church in a Latin cross shape,

was transformed by Antoni Gaudí into one of the world’s most ambitious and recognisable buildings. It combines Gothic aspiration, Christian symbolism, Catalan craft and forms drawn from nature. Columns branch like trees. Stone seems to grow.

The building’s high nave rises as a forest of tapering trunks reaching towards the canopy of light. There are 52 columns within, one for each Sunday of the year, holding up the high roof, and no flying buttresses despite its soaring height.
Outside, six stupendous towers now dominate

skyline, held up by the church’s 16 central columns. This is an engineering high-wire act of space-age ambition, all evolved by a model-building recluse in a workshop without computers or calculators.
New York’s Woolworth Building was nicknamed the ‘Cathedral of Commerce’ - Alamy/Felix Lipov
American know-how created skyscrapers: the safety elevator in New York and the steel frame in
. Early skyscrapers were Gothic. Pointing heavenwards, echoing medieval cathedrals, their vertical thrust was judged perfect for their scale and function.

Cass Gilbert’s mesmerising Woolworth Building emulated Charles Barry’s Victoria Tower in Westminster but is over twice the height. Limestone and terracotta-clad and immensely decorated with piers, pinnacles and ogee arches, the Woolworth Building briefly defined New York.
In an alternative, steam-punk world in which modernism never happened, skyscrapers would have been beautiful. Many might have emulated Gilbert’s Manhattan masterpiece.
Milan Central Railway Station features marble halls with decorative mosaics - iStockphoto/wsfurlan
Thank heavens the Victorians invented railways. Once upon a time, it was normal, indeed necessary, to create new infrastructure which was beautiful and functional.
The world’s most awe-inspiring railway terminus is probably the cavernous and effortlessly baroque Milano Centrale called
(Life in Motion) by its primary architect, Ulisse Stacchini. Walking through the stupendous portico and into the endless halls you feel suddenly at the wrong scale, like Alice in Wonderland.
Rashtrapati Bhavan, the former Viceroy’s House during the British Raj - saiko3p
Last and greatest of the British Empire’s physical creations, New Delhi’s government precinct is the world’s most successful instance of one man single-handedly creating a new architectural style.

Edwin Lutyens, very possibly England’s greatest ever architect, presided with others, notably Herbert Baker, helping with secondary buildings. Greatest of all is the Rashtrapati Bhavan, which, for 16 brief years, was the Viceroy’s House before the sun set on British rule.
Frauenkirche was reconstructed after RAF bombing in 1945 - Jorg Greuel

Dresden’s overwhelmingly beautiful Frauenkirche astonishes. Be-domed and baroque, it appears Catholic and 18th century. In fact, it is Lutheran and the church you see today is modern, the greatest building completed in our lifetimes.
Shattered by RAF bombing in 1945, a popular and locally led campaign

. Architects and elite left-wing opinion objected. But the people insisted. At the reconsecration, the packed congregation inside was joined by an estimated 60,000 townsfolk outside. Many wept. About two million visit each year. Join them.
Nicholas Boys Smith is the founder and chairman of Create Streets and visiting professor of architecture at the University of Strathclyde.
